column4: The section’s source root saʿy (س ع ي) names effort for earnings; this verse says a person has only what they strove for, making effort the basis of the allotment.
The section says the satisfied face looks back at its saʿy; this verse says that effort will be seen, so the work itself comes into view at judgment.
The section contrasts exhausting work with work that brings satisfaction; this verse completes the sequence by promising full recompense for effort.
The section calls saʿy work and earning; here those who seek the Hereafter and strive for it have saʿy that is acknowledged, the fulfilled counterpart to labor left only as fatigue.
The section’s pleased face is satisfied with its effort; in this garden scene the people are told their saʿy was appreciated, making the reward visible after hospitality.
The section joins effort with its reckoning; here no effort of a believer is denied and it is written down, so the reader sees both recognition and record.

The section names saʿy and describes work that yields only exhaustion; this verse says some people’s saʿy has gone astray while they think they did good work, with the root ḥ-s-b in their mistaken reckoning.
The section contrasts effort that is rewarded with effort that leaves only fatigue; here deeds are made scattered dust, a concrete image of work with no lasting return.
The section weighs whether effort yields a wage; this verse says God does not let the wage of one who does good work go to waste, the direct assurance opposite the futile labor.
The section links saʿy to the final reckoning; this verse says people will remember what they strove for on the day of the great event.
The section follows the worker’s effort to its reckoning; this verse portrays each person laboring toward the Lord and meeting Him, compressing effort and encounter into one scene.
The section’s worker expects a return for effort; this verse promises a good life and full wage for whoever does good work, male or female.
The section contrasts a laborer left only with fatigue and one satisfied with their effort; this verse describes full payment for work in worldly life, exposing a reward that may stop there.
The section asks whether work has a lasting return; this verse says the deeds of those who seek only worldly life come to nothing in the Hereafter.
The section divides faces by the result of their effort; this verse states that human saʿy is diverse, framing different labor and outcomes.
The section’s satisfied face has effort that yielded well; this verse begins the opposite path from futile labor, describing giving and God-consciousness.
The section weighs effort by what it yields; this verse describes affirming the good promise, the belief that accompanies the path of giving.
The section contrasts effort ending in strain with effort ending in satisfaction; this verse promises that the giver’s path will be made easy.
The section’s root gh-n-y (غ ن ي) appears in the idea of what does not suffice; here wealth will not avail its owner at the fall, a distinct but pointed form of insufficiency.
The section’s face is pleased with its effort; this verse sets against it the one who denies the good promise.
The section portrays effort that leaves a person exhausted; this verse says the path of the denier will be eased toward hardship.
The section treats saʿy as work with a return; this verse depicts giving wealth to purify oneself, an action whose aim is not immediate gain.
The section asks what a person’s effort earns; this verse says the giver seeks no repayment from anyone for a favor owed, clarifying the intended direction of the deed.
The section describes satisfaction with one’s effort and mutual approval; this verse makes seeking the face of the Most High the aim of giving.
The section’s pleased face sees a worthy result from its effort; this verse ends the giving passage with the giver becoming satisfied.
The section’s dictionary gloss nasīb (نصيب) is a share, and saʿy is work or earning; this verse joins a share to what people earned and says God is swift in reckoning.
The section hears a share in its root gloss for fatigue; this verse explicitly gives men and women a nasīb (نصيب) of what they earned, linking allotted share to labor.
The section’s nasīb (نصيب) gloss is an allotted share; this verse contrasts a share of the Hereafter’s harvest with having no share there for the one who seeks only this world.
The section ends with God’s account; this verse sets just scales on the Day of Resurrection and says even a mustard seed is not lost, showing how exact the reckoning is.
The section contrasts outcomes of effort; this verse places the true weighing on that Day and says the heavy scales belong to the successful.
The section’s successful effort yields satisfaction; this verse supplies the reverse side of the scales, where light weight means loss.
The section distinguishes effort by its final outcome; here heavy scales mark those who succeed at the reckoning.
The section sets satisfaction against wasted effort; here light scales leave their bearers lost, the adverse outcome to the heavy measure in 23:102.
The section’s account counts and evaluates; this verse makes the weighing of deeds the scene that determines each person’s outcome.
The section explicitly connects satisfaction with effort; this verse says the heavy-scaled person is in a pleasing life.
The section contrasts a pleased face with futile labor; this verse gives the opposite measure, the light scales.
The section’s contrasting efforts end in different states; this verse completes the light-scale outcome by naming its destination, Hāwiyah.
The section links work to the final account; this neighboring question introduces the consequence of the light scales named in 101:8.
The section contrasts satisfying and futile outcomes; this verse answers the preceding question with a blazing fire, completing the light-scale scene.
The section defines account as counting things; this verse says everything has been counted and recorded in a book.
The section names ḥ-s-b as counting and also cites its dictionary sense of sufficiency; this verse calls the recompense an adequate gift from the Lord.
The section ends with God’s account; this verse opens the book and says it leaves out neither small nor large deeds, which are found present without injustice.
The section describes a final account belonging to God; this verse says each person’s record will be brought out on the Day of Resurrection.
The section says ḥisāb (حساب) is counting things; here the person is told to read their book and is sufficient as their own reckoner.
The section says effort will be accounted for; this verse depicts people coming out in separate groups to be shown their deeds.
The section’s account takes each deed into view; this verse says even an atom’s weight of good will be seen.
The section contrasts efforts that satisfy and efforts that fail; this verse makes even an atom’s weight of evil visible too.
The section ties work to a final reckoning; this verse says every soul is paid in full for what it did and is not wronged.
The section ends by assigning the account to God; this verse says each soul is recompensed for what it earned and declares there is no injustice that Day.
The section’s work and its return meet in the final account; this verse says every soul is paid in full for what it did.
The section joins labor with recompense; this verse says every soul is repaid for what it earned without being wronged.
The section asks what each effort receives; this verse assigns people degrees according to their work and promises their deeds will be paid in full.
The section says the account is for the people’s deeds; this verse states that each person is repaid only for what they used to do.
The section contrasts worthwhile work with work that yields only fatigue; this verse distinguishes the multiplied return for good from the single measure of evil.
The section describes work becoming visible at the account; this verse says each soul will find present what good or evil it did.
The section treats effort as the basis of recompense; this verse says those who did evil and those who did good are repaid for what they did.
The section’s dictionary gloss for saʿy includes earning; this verse says each soul is held for what it earned.
The section contrasts reward with fruitless labor; this verse promises that believers’ deeds will not be diminished and that each person is held to what they earned.
The section hears laghw (لغو) as empty or excess speech and as what is dropped from an account; this verse says every utterance has a watcher ready, making the contrast with garden speech concrete.
The section’s dictionary branch for laghw (لغو) includes what is set aside from reckoning; this verse says there is no blame for laghw in oaths, but account is taken for deliberate binding.
The section links laghw (لغو) to speech excluded from an account; this verse distinguishes idle oaths, which are not held to account, from deliberate oaths that carry responsibility.
The section says no laghiya is heard in the garden; this verse likewise says its people will hear no idle speech there, only a greeting of peace.
The section’s garden has no laghw; this verse says there is neither idle speech nor sin in the garden scene.
The section describes a garden without laghiya; this verse says its people hear neither idle nor sinful speech there.
The section’s dictionary form laghw names empty speech and the garden is free of it; this verse says there is no idle talk or falsehood there.
The section’s word laghiya names empty speech; this verse portrays believers turning away from laghw, the worldly counterpart to a garden where it is not heard.
The section connects laghw with empty speech; this verse says the servants of the Merciful pass by such speech with dignity, a conduct parallel to its absence in the garden.
The section’s word laghiya is idle speech; this verse describes believers turning away when they hear laghw, a concrete response to the same kind of talk.
The section cites the joy of the person given the book from the right; this verse supplies that book-giving scene and starts the contrast of outcomes.
The section explicitly cites this speaker expecting to meet his ḥisāb (حساب); his confidence makes the account itself something anticipated rather than feared.
The section cites this person’s satisfied life after the account; it gives a concrete image of the return from the book and reckoning.
The section connects satisfied effort with a high garden; this verse places the person in a high garden after receiving the book.
The section’s satisfied face is in a garden; this neighboring verse makes its fruit near and accessible, a concrete sign of the reward.
The section says saʿy is labor or earning; this verse tells the garden people to eat and drink for what they sent ahead in earlier days.
The section sets the pleased account against futile effort; this verse begins the reversed book scene with the person receiving the record in the left hand.
The section explicitly cites the left-handed speaker who wishes not to know his ḥisāb (حساب), the adverse counterpart to the joyful meeting in 69:20.
The section’s root gh-n-y (غ ن ي) concerns what is sufficient; after the failed account, this speaker says his wealth did not avail him, a distinct but pointed failure of sufficiency.
The section contrasts two faces by their effort and outcome; this verse opens the parallel scene of receiving one’s book in the right hand.
The section ends with ḥisāb (حساب); this verse says the person will have an easy account, the favorable side of that reckoning.
The section’s face is pleased with its effort; this verse shows the right-handed person returning to their family rejoicing.
The section’s positive account has an opposite; this verse gives the other person’s book from behind their back.
The section contrasts satisfying and failed effort; this neighboring verse gives the despairing response to the adverse book, a wish for destruction.
The section contrasts the fates that follow effort; this verse completes the adverse book scene with entry into the blaze.
The section’s faces are divided by what their effort yields; this verse says the person in the adverse book had lived happily among their family before the return.
The section ends with a reckoning; this verse explains the contrast by the adverse person’s belief that they would not return.
The section says God owns the final account; this verse completes the book scene by saying the person’s Lord was watching them.
The section links effort and its final satisfaction; this verse calls to the tranquil soul as it returns to its Lord.
The section defines riḍā (رضا) as approval between servant and Lord; this verse describes the soul as pleased and pleasing as it returns.
The section’s satisfied soul is given a garden; this neighboring verse welcomes that soul among God’s servants.
The section links approval with garden reward; this neighboring verse completes the welcome by commanding the soul to enter the Garden.
The section defines mutual riḍā (رضا); this verse says God is pleased with the believers and they are pleased with Him, as their reward is gardens.
The section describes approval between servant and Lord; this verse applies that mutual pleasure to the foremost believers and promises gardens beneath which rivers flow.
The section’s riḍā gloss names the servant’s pleasure in God and God’s pleasure in the servant; this verse states that mutual approval on the Day when truth benefits.
The section joins the pleased servant with divine approval; this verse states both sides of that approval and pairs it with abiding gardens.
The section makes God’s pleasure part of the good return for effort; this verse calls divine approval greater than the gardens promised to believing men and women.
The section connects work with satisfaction in God; this verse describes a person who gives up himself seeking God’s approval.
The section’s satisfied face has a fitting effort; this verse contrasts following God’s approval with earning His anger.
The section treats effort as seeking a return; this verse depicts people feeding others for God’s sake without wanting recompense or thanks from them.
The section describes food that does not satisfy hunger; this verse gives another punishment meal, with no food except ghislin.
The section’s inadequate food belongs to a failed outcome; this neighboring verse says only sinners eat the punishment food in 69:36.
The section describes food that cannot relieve hunger; this verse gives the punished person choking food, another scene where eating is torment rather than provision.
The section contrasts garden reward with failed food; this verse asks whether the sinners’ welcome is the tree of Zaqqūm, a punishment meal.
The section’s failed food belongs to punishment; this neighboring verse locates the Zaqqūm tree at the root of Hell.
The section’s food scene is a sign of the failed outcome; this verse describes the frightening fruit of the punishment tree.
The section’s food does not nourish or satisfy hunger; this verse says the condemned eat from the tree and fill their bellies, a meal that fills without restoring them.
The section contrasts nourishment with hunger; this neighboring verse says the tree’s food is followed by a mixture of boiling water.
The section’s hungry face receives unusable food; this verse gives the condemned Zaqqūm as their food.
The section says its food does not satisfy hunger; this verse says the condemned fill their bellies with the punishment tree, which only loads the body before further torment.
The section contrasts nourishment with an unsatisfying meal; this neighboring verse follows the tree with boiling water to drink.
The section’s hunger is not relieved by its food; this verse completes the punishment-drink scene by comparing the drinking to thirsty camels.
The section’s food scene separates punishment from reward; this verse names Zaqqūm as the sinners’ food.
The section’s meal does not satisfy; this neighboring verse identifies Zaqqūm as the food of the sinner.
The section’s failed food is a punishment scene; this verse describes the tree’s contents boiling in the belly.
The section contrasts sustenance with torment; this verse completes the punishment-food image by comparing it to boiling water.
The section contrasts food that cannot sustain with a garden reward; this verse promises the garden people fruit and meat of what they desire.
The section’s food leaves hunger; this verse gives garden people fruit they choose, the provision opposite an unsatisfying meal.
The section’s hungry face has no satisfying food; this verse adds desired bird meat to the garden’s provision.
The section contrasts a drink that cannot help hunger with a good return; this verse gives the righteous a pure drink from their Lord.
The section’s nasīb (نصيب) is an allotted share; this verse speaks of one’s share in worldly life, distinguishing that limited portion from the enduring return discussed in the section.
The section makes the face that sees its effort and is satisfied visible; this verse portrays radiant faces on the Day of Resurrection, a parallel outward sign of a favorable outcome.
The section’s satisfied face turns toward its result; this verse depicts the radiant faces looking toward their Lord, without explicitly naming their deeds.
The section contrasts two kinds of face and the return of their efforts; this verse gives the opposite portrait of faces that day, gloomy.
The section’s adverse face ends in a failed outcome; this neighboring verse says those gloomy faces expect a backbreaking calamity.
The section follows a face’s effort to its final state; this verse shows radiant faces on that Day.
The section’s satisfied face is an outward sign of its return; this verse describes some faces as laughing and rejoicing.
The section divides faces by outcome; this verse begins the opposed portrait of dust-covered faces.
The section contrasts a satisfied result with a failed one; this verse says other faces are covered with darkness.
The section’s two faces mark divergent outcomes; this neighboring verse identifies the dust-covered, dark faces as those of disbelievers.
The section’s pleased face belongs to the successful effort; this verse promises those who do good the best reward and describes no gloom covering their faces.
The section contrasts satisfying effort with futile effort; this verse says those who earn evil have faces covered with humiliation.
The section opens its afterlife account with contrasting faces; this verse also depicts faces turning bright or dark, though it does not connect that appearance to effort.
The section’s two faces carry different outcomes; this verse completes the bright-face side by placing those faces in God’s mercy.
The section’s pleased face looks back at its effort; this verse makes the faces of the rewarded people recognizable by the radiance of bliss.
